paragraphs: Swamiji had a friend who owned a very fine painting. A wealthy man with a pious air had his heart set on it, but the friend refused to sell.
One day the wealthy man arrived with a solemn announcement: he had received an inspiration, a message straight from God. And what did God say? That the painting must be handed over to him.

The friend didn't miss a beat. How wonderful, he said, he had received exactly the same inspiration! Then he asked the visitor where his cheque was. The man was puzzled. The friend explained that his own message from God was quite specific: the painting was to go to the man who brought a cheque for $100,000. No cheque, no picture. Caught out, the visitor quietly dropped his talk of divine guidance.

Swamiji met a different kind of trouble in Boston. A man told him he had visions in which he was spoken to in the Hindu language. Swamiji said he would believe it if he could see what was said. The man wrote out pages of gibberish. Swamiji honestly tried to make sense of it, then told him that no such language had ever existed in India. The man left convinced that Swamiji was a rogue and a sceptic.
The world, Swamiji said, always holds these two dangers: frauds and fools. But that is no reason to hold back, because every great thing in this world comes with danger attached.
learn: Big spiritual or moral claims are easy to make and should be tested with common sense, especially when they happen to benefit the speaker. Stay open, but don't switch off your judgment.
